solutions.check: 24 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping); the blog's combined-key rows for 9A/3D, 23A/17A and 5D/14D each printed only the leading light's word (ARSE, EASY, COLD) and dropped the second word its own parsing already gave (AROUND, OPTION, SHOULDERED) — corrected from those parsings

clue.text: Blair in trouble — no good sounding off!

indicators.note: something in trouble has been knocked out of shape, and letters knocked out of shape do not stay in the order they were given

parts.note: the five letters of the name, rearranged
n.g. is the old shorthand for no good, pencilled on anything not up to scratch

explanation.surface: Blair in difficulty and no use to anyone, ranting away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sounding off' sits exactly where a homophone indicator would sit, and is the definition instead. The abbreviation is the sort setters keep alive long after the rest of us stopped writing it.
explanation.definitionFit: A blaring horn or a blaring voice is loud and refuses to be ignored, which is what sounding off describes.

clue.text: Dispatched soldiers again — Tony's main grudge

parts.note: re- is the prefix that means doing a thing over
to dispatch troops is to send them
an officer's men are his soldiers

indicators.note: the main letter of a name is its chief one, the initial it gets filed under

parts.note: the initial of the name

explanation.surface: Tony Blair's chief complaint, with troops posted abroad all over again.
explanation.walkthrough: Blair sending soldiers out twice over is the picture the surface paints. 'Again' in front of a verb is a prefix, and setters treat prefixes as charade pieces like any other.
explanation.definitionFit: Resentment is the ill-will you go on nursing long after the event, which is what holding a grudge amounts to.

clue.text: see 9ac.
Conservative purveyor of nonsense before poll — that's plain

parts.note: C is the letter printed beside a Tory candidate's name on a British ballot paper
Edward Lear wrote the Victorian nonsense verse every British child meets
to poll a hedge or a tree is to cut it back, which is where a pollard gets its name

explanation.surface: A Tory talking rubbish in the run-up to an election, and everyone can see it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poll' is the clue's second election word and the only one not doing election work. Edward Lear is the owl-and-the-pussycat man, which is how nonsense comes to have a surname.
explanation.definitionFit: Something clear-cut leaves no room for argument, which is 'plain' in the sense of obvious rather than unadorned.

clue.text: (& 14dn.) Corbyn, at first getting on, taken responsibility for — now frozen out

indicators.note: what a name is at first is the letter it opens with

parts.note: the opening letter of the name
somebody getting on in years is old
to shoulder the blame is to take responsibility for it

explanation.surface: An ageing Corbyn who carried the blame for everything and is now shut out.
explanation.walkthrough: Through the summer of 2016 Corbyn's own MPs resigned around him and then tried to unseat him, so the surface is the news of the week. The answer runs on into 14 down.
explanation.definitionFit: To cold-shoulder someone is to freeze them out — deliberate, chilly exclusion rather than an open quarrel.

clue.text: Fast arranged by old failed candidate and member with alternative backing

indicators.note: what is backing is travelling the other way, so those two letters are written in reverse

parts.note: Al Gore lost the 2000 US presidential election, and his first name is all that is wanted
an arm or a leg is a member of the body
OR is the alternative word, here written the other way round

explanation.surface: A brisk piece put together by a beaten candidate and an MP funded from elsewhere.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Arranged by' does musical duty in the surface and joining duty in the wordplay, and the answer is a tempo marking rather than a piece of music. 'Member' is the crossword's arm or leg, not the man in the Commons.
explanation.definitionFit: Allegro is the instruction at the head of a score telling the player to take it fast.

clue.text: Scottish leader's first to go far right — nuts

definitions.note: a plural noun, matching the answer

indicators.note: the first letter is moved all the way to the right-hand end, with a political pun on the far right

parts.note: Alex Salmond was the leader of the Scottish National Party and First Minister of Scotland

explanation.surface: A jibe that a Scottish nationalist leader drifting to the far right would be mad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nuts' looks like an insult, but it is the definition, in its literal food sense. Moving the S of SALMOND to the end gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Almonds are the edible kernels of the almond tree, one of the commonest kinds of nut.

clue.text: Help the party — party Corbyn finally chewed up?

indicators.note: what comes finally comes last, so the name hands over only the letter it closes with

parts.note: a do is a party, the British word for any organised knees-up
the last letter of the name
whoever has chewed something up has eaten it

explanation.surface: Chip in for the party — the bash Corbyn finally devoured.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chewed up' sits exactly where an anagram indicator belongs and turns out to be a past tense. The dash is all that separates the definition from the wordplay, and both sides begin with the same word.
explanation.definitionFit: To donate is to give money, and money is the help a political party asks for before anything else.

clue.text: (& 3dn.) Prats do "Cyclops-like ears"

definitions.note: a prat is a fool, and what fools do is fool about

parts.note: EARS as this bawdy setter might clue it: a rude word for bottom followed by an anagram signal, so the answer read as wordplay jumbles that word into the clue's word

explanation.surface: Fools mock someone with odd ears, the Cyclops being famous for one strange feature.
explanation.walkthrough: This works backwards: 'Cyclops-like' says the answer is how this setter would clue EARS, with AROUND acting on ARSE to rearrange it.
explanation.definitionFit: To arse around is British slang for messing about foolishly, which is typical behaviour of prats, idiots.

clue.text: Ethical — so finished being a candidate?

parts.note: when time is up it is finished
in Britain a candidate stands for a seat where an American would run for it

explanation.surface: So decent a man that putting himself forward for election finishes him.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark owns the joke that being ethical is what ends a political career. 'Stand' is the British verb for putting your name on a ballot paper, and it hides in plain sight.
explanation.definitionFit: An upstanding citizen is honest and straight-dealing, which is the ethical sense the clue wants.

clue.text: One who needs to get a firm grip, Labour's leader, being in ever weird situation

definitions.text: One who needs to get a firm grip

indicators.note: whatever is being in something sits inside it, between its letters

parts.note: a situation that is ever weirder is a stranger one, and 'ever' is what forces the comparative
the leading letter of the word Labour

explanation.surface: A Labour leader flailing in an ever odder situation and needing to take control.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get a grip' is what you say to somebody panicking, and the definition wants the literal pair of hands instead. Comparatives are quietly useful to setters: 'weird' with 'ever' in front of it becomes a different word.
explanation.definitionFit: Strangling is done with the hands, so the definition describes the job by its one professional requirement rather than naming it.

clue.text: Not like Miliband to have magnetism, agreed?

indicators.note: what a thing has, it holds inside it, so the letters named next go into the middle

parts.note: not Ed: UN for not, and Ed Miliband led Labour from 2010 to 2015
'it' is the coy old word for sex appeal, as in the It girl

explanation.surface: It would be unlike Ed Miliband to have any sex appeal, wouldn't you say?
explanation.walkthrough: The It girl was Clara Bow in the 1920s, and setters have never let the usage go. The whole surface is a dig at Miliband's charisma, and the tag question at the end is doing the defining.
explanation.definitionFit: A party that is united is agreed — of one mind, with the argument over.

clue.text: It certainly has the money to distribute Boris etching — boing, gone!

indicators.note: to distribute is to spread around, so the letters are scattered into a new order
gone means departed, so the letters of that word leave the pool before the rearrangement

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Boris Johnson's artwork is sold off by wealthy buyers, and boing, it vanishes.
explanation.walkthrough: Pool the letters of BORIS and ETCHING, take away those of BOING (signalled by 'gone'), and rearrange the rest. 'boing' is Boris Johnson's catchphrase exclamation.
explanation.definitionFit: The rich set is the wealthy social class, a group which by definition has plenty of cash.

clue.text: see 5dn.
Response of some leaders to Brexit crisis might be put into words as "We'll just have to lump it"

definitions.text: Response of some leaders to Brexit crisis
definitions.note: The second definition is a line of speech rather than a synonym, which the clue admits by asking you to put the word into words.
definitions.meaning: quitting the job — what David Cameron did the morning after the June 2016 referendum, with others following him out

definitions.text: We'll just have to lump it
definitions.meaning: the shrug of somebody who has accepted an outcome they cannot change

explanation.surface: How certain leaders reacted to the referendum result, put as a weary shrug.
explanation.walkthrough: Cameron announced he was going the morning after the vote. The two halves are one word in two moods — an act you perform and an attitude you settle into.
explanation.definitionFit: Resignation is both the letter a leader hands in and the mood of putting up with what cannot be helped.

clue.text: How a male peer's task is completed quickly

parts.words: How a male peer's task is completed
parts.note: the surface offers a lord in ermine getting through his business in the Lords; said aloud he is a male pee-er, and the task at the urinal is finished with a shake

explanation.surface: A peer of the realm getting through his parliamentary duties.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Peer' is the pivot: say it aloud as pee-er and the task stops being parliamentary. The phrase itself is the older half of 'two shakes of a lamb's tail'.
explanation.definitionFit: A shake is the smallest unit of time the phrase has to offer, so doing a thing in one is doing it at once.

clue.text: see 23ac.
Main conclusion of Boris: "Yuk! What one gets from boat-rocking!"

parts.note: the main is the open sea, the word that survives in the Spanish Main

indicators.note: the conclusion of a name is where it stops, which is its final letter

parts.note: the last letter of the name
the other noise of disgust, spelt as it is said

explanation.surface: Boris signing off with a disgusted verdict on what rocking the boat brings.
explanation.walkthrough: Rocking the boat is normally the metaphor for making trouble, and here the boat is literal. 'Main' for the open sea has survived in the Spanish Main and in crosswords, and almost nowhere else.
explanation.definitionFit: Being seasick is what a rocking boat does to you, and the word carries the queasiness rather than the vessel.

clue.text: Danger when PM misses Brexit climax and collapse

indicators.note: what a word misses it does not have, so that letter goes before anything is joined on
the climax is the high point at the end, so the word gives up the letter it finishes with

parts.note: William Pitt, Prime Minister twice over before 1806
the last letter of BREXIT, which is the one taken out
a collapse is a fall

explanation.surface: The Prime Minister missing the Brexit finale, and everything falling apart.
explanation.walkthrough: Pitt is the Prime Minister crosswords reach for, because the name is short and there were two of him, father and son. 'Climax' is asking for a position in a word rather than an event.
explanation.definitionFit: A pitfall was first a covered pit dug to trap animals, so it is danger you do not see until you are in it.

clue.text: Rejected grass, um … as a hairstyle

indicators.note: something rejected is thrown back, and letters thrown back are read the other way

parts.note: to grass on someone is to tell on them, and TELL with the hesitation noise after it is read backwards

explanation.surface: Turf turned down, with some hesitation, offered as a way to wear your hair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grass' is the informer's sense here, not the lawn the surface plants. The trailing dots are the hesitation going on a moment longer, and they are worth no letters at all.
explanation.definitionFit: A mullet is the haircut that is short at the front and long at the back, so the clue names its category and lets the wordplay do the rest.

clue.text: May, getting reduced party backing, er, needs new go-ahead

indicators.note: getting reduced means cut down, here to just its first letter
backing means going backwards, so the word for party is read in reverse

parts.note: a do is a party

explanation.surface: Theresa May, with her party's support dwindling, hesitantly asks for fresh permission to carry on.
explanation.walkthrough: May is Theresa May, the former Prime Minister. 'getting reduced' cuts her down to M, 'backing' turns DO round, and ER and N follow. 'er' is just the hesitation, taken as written.
explanation.definitionFit: Go-ahead used as an adjective means progressive and enterprising, which is close to modern in outlook.

clue.text: Welcome a beating, as masochists might do affectionately at the opening of parliament?

definitions.text: Welcome a beating, as masochists might do

parts.note: the affectionate greeting itself
Black Rod is the official who marches to the Commons door at every State Opening, and he is known simply as the Rod

explanation.surface: Masochists looking forward to a thrashing at the State Opening of Parliament.
explanation.walkthrough: Black Rod has the Commons door slammed in his face at every State Opening before the MPs troop after him to the Lords, so the ceremony supplies a person as well as a date.
explanation.definitionFit: To kiss the rod is to take your punishment meekly, the rod being the stick you were beaten with.

clue.text: Senior Corbynite starts to put over Sturgeon?

indicators.note: starts means the beginnings, so the first letter of each word is taken

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: put over means turned over, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A senior Corbyn supporter begins to win over Nicola Sturgeon.
explanation.walkthrough: Nicola Sturgeon is a former First Minister of Scotland, so she is an example of the answer; the question mark marks that. 'starts' gives SC, and 'put over' turns TO round.
explanation.definitionFit: Nicola Sturgeon, long-time SNP leader, is Scottish, so she is one example of a Scot.

clue.text: (& 17dn.) A tempting alternative, possibly, to a penis, without a call for attention

indicators.note: without in its old sense means outside, so the jumbled letters go around the call
possibly says the letters could be arranged another way

parts.note: taken as written
yo is an informal call for someone's attention

explanation.surface: A crude joke about what might be tempting instead of sex, minus the shout to get attention.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' looks like it means 'lacking', but here it means outside: the rearranged letters of TO A PENIS go round YO.
explanation.definitionFit: An easy option is the less demanding choice, a tempting alternative to doing the harder thing.

clue.text: Sun spread including "Phwoar! Knickers capital!" gets it in the neck? The opposite

definitions.text: gets it in the neck? The opposite
definitions.note: The definition is inverted: the phrase names what the answer undoes, and 'The opposite' turns it round.

indicators.note: a thing spread out has been opened up, and its letters no longer sit where they did
what a word includes it holds inside itself

parts.note: the three letters of SUN rearranged, then opened up round the middle
cor is the politer British noise of appreciation that phwoar belongs to

indicators.note: the capital of a word is the big letter it starts with

parts.note: the big letter the word starts with

explanation.surface: A Sun centre spread with a leering headline about underwear, and somebody catching the blame.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gets it in the neck' means taking the blame, and the answer will have none of it: the neck here belongs to a bottle. 'Capital' is a letter rather than a city, which is the joke in 'Knickers capital'.
explanation.definitionFit: A cork goes into the neck of a bottle, so the answer, which pulls it out again, is the opposite of getting it in the neck.

clue.text: Haste of press to stand against Cameron's ultimate hollow "clarity"

indicators.note: to stand against is to be placed next to, so the pieces are set side by side in this order

parts.note: to urge is to press someone

indicators.note: ultimate means last, so the final letter of the name is taken

parts.note: the name Cameron, with the possessive ignored

indicators.note: hollow means emptied of its inside, so only the outer letters are left

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A rushed press campaign against David Cameron's empty promises of clarity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'press' reads as the newspapers, but it is the verb URGE. N ends CAMERON, and 'hollow' leaves CY of 'clarity'.
explanation.definitionFit: Urgency means pressing need for swift action, which is what haste implies.
